title: Hello
description: Greet someone, and be polite about it.
grammarNote: Good morning is only for the morning. Good afternoon is for the afternoon, and good night is for the evening.

explanation.summary: Greeting someone in Spanish is mostly a matter of picking the right phrase for the time of day. Hola works at any hour, and the rest are built around buenos and buenas.

sections.heading: The three good ones
sections.body: Buenos días is for the morning, buenas tardes for the afternoon, and buenas noches for the evening. The adjective agrees: buenos and buenas. The noun that goes with them is singular, and that is what makes them look odd: literally good days, good afternoon and good evenings.

sections.heading: Saying hello and goodbye
sections.body: Hola works at any time of day, and it is the safest greeting. Adiós is a goodbye for leaving or ending a conversation. Hasta luego is see you later, and it works for leaving. Adiós carries a slight formality that hasta luego does not.

sections.heading: Being polite
sections.body: Gracias is thank you, and it never changes. De nada is the answer, and it means literally it is nothing. Por favor goes before the thing you are asking for: un café, por favor. Yes is sí, with an accent, and no is no.

examples.es: Un café con leche, por favor.

items.note: Hello. It is used at any time of day.
Goodbye. The accent marks the stress.
Good afternoon. It also means good evening.
Thank you. It never changes form.
Please. It always comes before what you are asking for.
Yes. The accent marks the stress.
How is it going. It is an informal greeting.

drills.note: Por favor goes before the thing you are asking for.
De nada is the answer to gracias.
